title: Summarize Basic Cable Types and Their Connectors, Features, and Purposes

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Different cables carry network data, peripheral data, video, storage traffic, or power. Objective 3.2 tests whether you can connect the medium and purpose to the correct cable and physical connector.
The central workflow is: identify what the connection carries, select the cable or interface family, and then recognize the connector.
sections.callout: WHAT IS IT CARRYING? → WHAT CABLE? → WHAT CONNECTOR?

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes a cable's medium, connector, performance generation, installation environment, or purpose, identify the exact cable or connector before choosing an answer.
bullets: Modern reversible data, power, or compatible video → USB-C
Digital or analog video → HDMI, DisplayPort, DVI, VGA, or USB-C

sections.title: Network Cables
paragraphs: Network cables carry data between networked devices. The named media are copper, coaxial, twisted pair, and optical fiber.
sections.callout: Electrical signal → copper. Light → optical fiber.

sections.title: Copper Network Cabling
paragraphs: Copper Network Cabling carries electrical signals. Objective 3.2 includes twisted-pair Ethernet and coaxial cable, with twisted pair further distinguished by category, shielding, and installation rating.
sections.callout: Copper = electrical signal.

sections.title: Cable Categories
paragraphs: Cable Categories identify performance and construction classes for twisted-pair Ethernet. Common examples include Cat 5e, Cat 6, and Cat 6a.
bullets: Higher categories support newer or higher-performance Ethernet specifications when correctly installed.
NICs, switches, connectors, run length, and installation quality also affect actual link performance.
sections.callout: Category = cable capability class, not the connector name.

sections.title: T568A and T568B Standards
paragraphs: T568A/T568B Standards define the conductor color order used when terminating twisted-pair Ethernet. Both use eight conductors, but the orange and green pair positions differ.
sections.callout: Ethernet conductor color sequence → T568A or T568B.

sections.title: Straight-Through Cabling
paragraphs: A straight-through cable uses the same termination standard on both ends: T568A to T568A or T568B to T568B. Modern Ethernet ports often handle crossover needs automatically, but consistent termination remains essential.
sections.callout: Same pattern on both ends → straight-through cable.

sections.title: Shielded Twisted Pair
paragraphs: Shielded Twisted Pair (STP) adds shielding to reduce electromagnetic interference and radio-frequency interference. It is useful near motors, industrial equipment, or other electrically noisy systems.
sections.callout: High-interference Ethernet environment → STP.

sections.title: Unshielded Twisted Pair
paragraphs: Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) does not include the additional shielding used by STP. It is the common choice for ordinary office and home Ethernet installations.
sections.callout: Typical everyday Ethernet → UTP.

sections.title: STP vs. UTP
sections.callout: Noise → STP. Normal environment → UTP.

sections.title: Direct Burial Cable
paragraphs: Direct Burial Cable has protective construction for underground installation and exposure to moisture, soil, and outdoor conditions.
sections.callout: Underground network run → direct burial cable.

sections.title: Plenum-Rated Cable
paragraphs: Plenum-Rated Cable is designed for building air-handling spaces. Its jacket reduces dangerous smoke and toxic emissions compared with ordinary cable when exposed to fire.
sections.callout: GROUND → direct burial. AIR-HANDLING SPACE → plenum-rated.

sections.title: Coaxial Cable
paragraphs: Coaxial cable has a central conductor surrounded by insulation, shielding, and an outer jacket. It is commonly used for cable television, cable internet, and cable-modem connections.
sections.callout: Cable modem or cable television medium → coaxial.

sections.title: Optical Cabling
paragraphs: Optical Cabling transmits data as light rather than electrical signals. Fiber supports high bandwidth and long distances and is resistant to electromagnetic interference.
sections.callout: Light rather than electricity → optical fiber.

sections.title: Single-Mode Fiber
paragraphs: Single-Mode Fiber uses a small core and a single primary light path. It is suited to very long distances, provider links, and backbone connectivity.
sections.callout: Long-distance optical link → single-mode fiber.

sections.title: Multimode Fiber
paragraphs: Multimode Fiber uses a larger core and supports multiple light paths. It is commonly used for shorter-distance links within buildings and data centers.
sections.callout: Shorter local optical link → multimode fiber.

sections.title: Single-Mode vs. Multimode
sections.callout: SINGLE = FAR. MULTI = NEARER.

sections.title: Peripheral Cables
paragraphs: Peripheral Cables connect computers to external devices. Objective 3.2 names USB 2.0, USB 3.0, serial cable, and Thunderbolt.
sections.callout: Identify the interface generation separately from the connector shape.

sections.title: USB 2.0
paragraphs: USB 2.0 is an older Universal Serial Bus generation used by keyboards, mice, printers, storage devices, and other peripherals. It carries data and can provide power.
sections.callout: Older common USB performance generation → USB 2.0.

sections.title: USB 3.0
paragraphs: USB 3.0 provides substantially higher transfer capability than USB 2.0 and is commonly used for external storage, docks, and high-speed peripherals.
sections.callout: Higher-throughput USB generation → USB 3.0.

sections.title: USB 2.0 vs. USB 3.0
sections.callout: USB version = capability. USB connector name = physical shape.

sections.title: Serial Cable
paragraphs: A Serial Cable is associated with legacy peripherals, console connections, and industrial equipment. A common legacy serial connector is the 9-pin D-sub DB9.
sections.callout: Legacy communications or nine-pin D-shaped connector → serial/DB9.

sections.title: Thunderbolt
paragraphs: Thunderbolt is a high-speed multipurpose interface that can carry high-speed data, display traffic, docking connections, and external-storage traffic. Modern versions commonly use a USB-C connector shape.
sections.callout: USB-C shape does not automatically guarantee Thunderbolt support.

sections.title: Video Cables
paragraphs: Video Cables carry display signals. The named interfaces are High-Definition Multimedia Interface, DisplayPort, Digital Visual Interface, Video Graphics Array, and compatible USB-C video.
sections.callout: Determine whether the clue calls for consumer digital, PC digital, older display, analog legacy, or USB-C video.

sections.title: High-Definition Multimedia Interface
paragraphs: High-Definition Multimedia Interface (HDMI) carries digital video and audio. It is common on televisions, monitors, game consoles, laptops, and media devices.
sections.callout: One digital cable carries picture and sound to a television → HDMI.

sections.title: DisplayPort
paragraphs: DisplayPort is a digital display interface common on PCs, graphics cards, and computer monitors. It supports digital video and can also carry audio.
sections.callout: PC-focused digital monitor connection → DisplayPort.

sections.title: Digital Visual Interface
paragraphs: Digital Visual Interface (DVI) is an older computer-display interface. Depending on the DVI variant, it can carry digital video, analog video, or both.
sections.callout: Older PC display connector from the digital era → DVI.

sections.title: Video Graphics Array
paragraphs: Video Graphics Array (VGA) is a legacy analog video interface commonly associated with a 15-pin D-shaped connector.
sections.callout: Legacy analog monitor connection → VGA.

sections.title: USB-C for Video
paragraphs: USB-C Video can carry a display signal when the device, port, cable, and supported display mode or protocol provide that capability. The same connector shape may also carry data and power.
sections.callout: USB-C shape does not guarantee video, speed, power, or Thunderbolt capabilities.

sections.title: HDMI vs. DisplayPort vs. DVI vs. VGA

table.caption: Video-interface recognition
rows: Digital video and audio; consumer AV

sections.callout: HDMI = TV/AV. DisplayPort = PC digital. DVI = older PC. VGA = analog legacy.

sections.title: Hard Drive Cables
paragraphs: Hard Drive Cables connect storage devices. Objective 3.2 distinguishes internal Serial Advanced Technology Attachment from External SATA.
sections.callout: Inside the computer → SATA. External SATA device → eSATA.

sections.title: Serial Advanced Technology Attachment
paragraphs: Serial Advanced Technology Attachment (SATA) connects internal hard drives, SATA solid-state drives, and optical drives. A SATA drive commonly uses separate data and power connections.
sections.callout: Internal drive data connection to the motherboard → SATA cable.

sections.title: External SATA
paragraphs: External SATA (eSATA) extends SATA connectivity to external storage devices.
sections.callout: SATA outside the computer → eSATA cable.

sections.title: SATA vs. eSATA
sections.callout: SATA = inside. eSATA = outside.

sections.title: Adapters
paragraphs: Adapters connect unlike physical interfaces when the underlying signals and conversion are compatible. Examples include USB-C to HDMI, DisplayPort to HDMI, USB to Ethernet, and compatible DVI conversions.
sections.callout: Different connectors with supported conversion → adapter.

sections.title: Connector Types
paragraphs: Connector Types describe the physical termination or receptacle. Do not confuse a connector shape with a cable category, data standard, or guaranteed capability.
sections.callout: Cable category and interface version describe capability; connector name describes physical form.

sections.title: RJ11
paragraphs: RJ11 is commonly associated with telephone connections and is physically smaller than RJ45.
sections.callout: Telephone-line connector → RJ11.

sections.title: RJ45
paragraphs: RJ45 is the common modular connector associated with twisted-pair Ethernet.
sections.callout: Cat 5e, Cat 6, or Cat 6a Ethernet plug → RJ45.

sections.title: RJ11 vs. RJ45
sections.callout: Phone = RJ11. Network = RJ45.

sections.title: F-Type Connector
paragraphs: The F-Type connector is a screw-on connector used with coaxial cable for cable television and cable-modem connections.
sections.callout: Coaxial cable connection → F-type.

sections.title: Straight Tip
paragraphs: Straight Tip (ST) is a fiber-optic connector with a bayonet-style twist-lock mechanism.
sections.callout: Fiber connector that twists and locks → ST.

sections.title: Subscriber Connector
paragraphs: Subscriber Connector (SC) is a square-profile fiber connector with a push-pull design.
sections.callout: Push-pull fiber connector → SC.

sections.title: Lucent Connector
paragraphs: Lucent Connector (LC) is a small-form-factor fiber connector used where high connector density matters.
sections.callout: Small, dense fiber connector → LC.

sections.title: ST vs. SC vs. LC
sections.callout: ST = TWIST. SC = PUSH. LC = LITTLE.

sections.title: Punchdown Block
paragraphs: A Punchdown Block provides termination points for individual copper conductors. A punchdown tool seats the wires into insulation-displacement slots.
sections.callout: Terminate individual twisted-pair conductors → punchdown block.

sections.title: MicroUSB
paragraphs: MicroUSB is a small USB connector commonly found on older mobile devices and peripherals.
sections.callout: Older small mobile USB connector → MicroUSB.

sections.title: MiniUSB
paragraphs: MiniUSB is an older USB connector that is larger than MicroUSB and appeared on cameras, GPS units, and other earlier electronics.
sections.callout: Older USB connector larger than MicroUSB → MiniUSB.

sections.title: USB-C Connector
paragraphs: The USB-C Connector is compact and reversible. Depending on the implementation, it may support data, power, charging, video, or Thunderbolt.
sections.callout: Reversible modern connector; capabilities must be verified separately → USB-C.

sections.title: Molex
paragraphs: Molex is a legacy internal power connector used with older hard drives, optical drives, fans, and other internal components.
sections.callout: Legacy four-pin internal peripheral power → Molex.

sections.title: Lightning Connector
paragraphs: The Lightning Connector is a proprietary reversible connector associated with many earlier Apple mobile devices. Newer Apple devices may use USB-C instead.
sections.callout: Earlier Apple mobile connector → Lightning.

sections.title: DB9
paragraphs: DB9 is a 9-pin D-sub connector commonly associated with serial communication.
sections.callout: Nine-pin legacy serial connector → DB9.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Consumer digital audio and video → HDMI

sections.title: Objective 3.2 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Similar-looking cables and connectors are separated by medium, purpose, environment, generation, or physical form. Identify those categories before choosing.

entries.title: RJ11 vs. RJ45
paragraphs: RJ11 is telephone; RJ45 is Ethernet.

entries.title: STP vs. UTP
paragraphs: STP adds interference shielding; UTP is common for normal environments.

entries.title: Direct Burial vs. Plenum
paragraphs: Direct burial solves underground exposure; plenum rating addresses air-handling fire and smoke requirements.

entries.title: Single-Mode vs. Multimode
paragraphs: Single-mode is the long-distance clue; multimode is the shorter-distance clue.

entries.title: T568 Standard vs. Cable Category
paragraphs: T568A/T568B define conductor order; Cat 5e, Cat 6, and Cat 6a are cable categories.

entries.title: USB Generation vs. Connector
paragraphs: USB 2.0 and USB 3.0 are performance generations; MicroUSB, MiniUSB, and USB-C are connector forms.

entries.title: USB-C vs. Thunderbolt
paragraphs: USB-C is a connector shape; Thunderbolt is an interface technology that may use USB-C.

entries.title: HDMI vs. DisplayPort
paragraphs: Both carry digital display traffic; HDMI is common in consumer AV, while DisplayPort is common on PCs and monitors.

entries.title: DVI vs. VGA
paragraphs: DVI is an older computer-display interface; VGA is legacy analog video.

entries.title: SATA vs. eSATA
paragraphs: SATA is internal; eSATA is external.

entries.title: SATA Data vs. Molex Power
paragraphs: SATA is the storage data interface; Molex is a legacy power connector.

entries.title: ST vs. SC vs. LC
paragraphs: ST twists, SC pushes, and LC is the small-form-factor fiber connector.

sections.callout: MEDIUM → PURPOSE → CONNECTOR.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: HDMI → digital consumer audio and video
USB-C → reversible connector with implementation-dependent capabilities
NETWORK → RJ45, F-TYPE, or FIBER; PHONE → RJ11; VIDEO → HDMI, DISPLAYPORT, DVI, VGA, or USB-C; STORAGE → SATA or eSATA; SERIAL → DB9; POWER → MOLEX
